scenes.title: The compute fragmentation problem
scenes.narration: Modern systems span phones, edge devices, workstations, and cloud infrastructure. Yet workloads are often scheduled without a unified view of capacity, latency, locality, trust, and cost.

scenes.title: One fabric. Explicit placement.
scenes.narration: Universal Compute Fabric, or UCF, is an experimental control plane for coordinating workloads across registered heterogeneous nodes.

scenes.title: How UCF works
scenes.narration: A control plane maintains node inventory, heartbeats, leases, and capacity. Its scheduler places explicit tasks on eligible nodes. Workers claim assigned tasks, execute them, and report completion through authenticated APIs.

scenes.title: Designed around real constraints
scenes.narration: UCF keeps safety-critical control and offline fallback local. It treats network memory as remote, not as local process RAM. Optional container execution is disabled by default and restricted to pre-approved image digests.

scenes.title: Business value
scenes.narration: The intended value is a measurable foundation for using existing compute more deliberately: improving resource visibility, testing workload placement strategies, and evaluating latency, energy, bandwidth, and cost per active user.

scenes.title: Experimental by design
scenes.narration: UCF is an M2 experimental execution foundation, not a universal remote CPU or production multi-tenant platform. Stronger identity, tenant isolation, attestation, hardened execution, and recovery remain future work. Review the architecture and roadmap on GitHub.
